title: Dynamic Induction of Lattice Gauge Theories on a Quantum Computer
authors: Barbara Andrade, Declan Millar, Lewis Anderson, Vincent R. Pascuzzi, Maciej Lewenstein, Ivano Tavernelli, Jad C. Halimeh, Tobias Grass
abstract: Gauge invariance is central to modern physics and underpins quantum simulations of lattice gauge theories (LGTs). Existing quantum simulation approaches employ Gauss's law either to energetically suppress gauge-violating processes in analog platforms or to detect and discard gauge-violating outcomes in digital devices. Here we introduce a third paradigm, in which Gauss's law is used to dynamically generate the gauge theory itself from a substantially simpler Hamiltonian. Starting from a readily programmable three-body XXX model, we employ experimentally efficient single-qubit U(1) gauge symmetry-generator terms that induce the dynamics of a U(1) LGT. We implement this approach using 101 qubits on a 156-qubit IBM quantum processor and observe real-time dynamics in quantitative agreement with the target LGT while reducing the entangling-gate depth per Trotter step by a factor of five compared with a direct implementation. Our results establish gauge protection as a resource for Hamiltonian engineering rather than merely symmetry preservation, opening a scalable resource-efficient route towards digital quantum simulations of increasingly complex gauge theories in higher spatial dimensions.
summary: The paper introduces a breakthrough method to simulate Lattice Gauge Theories on quantum computers by dynamically generating the required gauge dynamics from a simpler starting Hamiltonian. By using single-qubit terms derived from Gauss's law, they successfully confine the evolution to the physical subspace while drastically reducing the circuit depth compared to direct simulation methods.
main_problem: Developing a resource-efficient method for digital quantum simulation of Lattice Gauge Theories (LGTs) while rigorously enforcing gauge invariance.
main_result: The authors demonstrated that using single-qubit terms proportional to the Gauss's law generator can dynamically induce the LGT dynamics from a simpler Hamiltonian, achieving a fivefold reduction in entangling-gate depth compared to direct implementations.
method: They employ a novel 'dynamic induction' paradigm where gauge constraints are enforced via experimentally efficient single-qubit penalty terms ($V_{HG}$) added to a simple starting Hamiltonian ($H_{XXX}$), rather than relying on post-selection or energy penalties.
model_or_system: The target system is the U(1) Quantum Link Model (QLM) LGT, simulated using spin-1/2 qubits. The implementation uses 101 qubits on an IBM quantum processor to simulate dynamics in $1+1$ dimensions.
key_observables: Average gauge violation ($\langle \epsilon_G angle$), mean electric field ($\langle E angle$), and comparison of time evolution against Matrix Product State (MPS) classical benchmarks.
important_parameters: Gauge protection strength ($V=4.5$); Trotter step size ($\Delta t=0.25$); Lattice size ($N_f=50$).
main_assumptions: The method is shown to work for $1+1$ dimensions, and the initial Hamiltonian used is simpler than the full target LGT.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate qubit encoding, gauge protection mechanisms separating physical/unphysical sectors, and time evolution plots comparing protected vs. unprotected dynamics of observables like $\langle \epsilon_G angle$ and $\langle E angle$.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem (LGT simulation), proposes the dynamic induction method using $H_{XXX}$ plus gauge terms ($V_{HG}$), details the implementation on quantum hardware, presents results showing reduced circuit depth and accurate dynamics matching classical benchmarks.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses resource limitations in simulating complex physical theories like LGTs by transforming a symmetry constraint into an active, efficient part of the Hamiltonian engineering process, which is highly relevant for quantum simulation algorithms.
